title: Tunnels: carrying one network inside another
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what a tunnel actually does to a packet, say what a VPN does and does not protect, and choose between a full tunnel and a split tunnel for a given purpose.

blocks.text: A tunnel takes a complete packet, treats it as data, and puts it inside another packet. The outer packet travels the ordinary internet; at the far end the inner packet is unwrapped and released as if it had originated there. That is the whole mechanism, and every VPN is an application of it.

blocks.caption: What the layers lesson described, applied deliberately
lines: [ IP: you -> server ][ TCP ][ your data ]
The same packet through a tunnel:
[ IP: you -> VPN gateway ][ encrypted ][ IP: you -> server ][ TCP ][ your data ]
|___ what the network sees ___||_________ what only the endpoints see _______|
/* The network between you and the gateway sees one connection,
to one address, carrying opaque bytes. The inner packet is invisible. */

blocks.text: That extra header has a size, which is why a VPN connection has a smaller usable packet size than the link it runs over — and why the MTU problems from the layers lesson appear so often on VPNs specifically. If large transfers hang over a tunnel and small ones work, that is the first thing to check.
What a VPN actually gives you

rows: Your traffic from the local network and its operator
Your traffic from the VPN provider — you moved the trust, not removed it
Which sites you visit, from your internet provider
Your identity from sites you log into
Your address from the sites you visit
Anything the site learns from cookies, fingerprinting, or your account
A connection back into a private network
Against malware, phishing, or a compromised device

blocks.title: A VPN moves trust; it does not eliminate it
blocks.text: Without one, your internet provider can see which sites you connect to. With one, they see only the tunnel — and the VPN provider now sees what they used to. That is a real improvement on a public network you do not trust, and it is not anonymity. The clearest way to think about it: you are choosing whose logs you appear in.
Two shapes, for two different jobs

rows: Untrusted networks; policy requiring all traffic inspected
Reaching a company network while working normally otherwise

blocks.text: The difference is entirely a matter of routing, and you can see it: a full tunnel installs a default route through the tunnel interface, so the longest-prefix rule from the routing lesson sends everything there. A split tunnel installs only specific routes, so everything else continues to use the original default.

rows: Which server, but not the content
Your device and the VPN gateway
One tunnel; beyond the gateway, ordinary traffic

blocks.title: A VPN does not make an unencrypted site safe
blocks.text: Traffic is protected only as far as the gateway. Past that point it continues as it otherwise would — so a plain http site is still plain http on the second half of the journey. This is worth being clear about because it is a common misunderstanding: end-to-end encryption and tunnel encryption protect different segments, and only the first covers the whole path.
Related uses of the same idea

items: Site-to-site: two office networks joined so machines address each other as if local
Remote access: one device joining a private network from anywhere
Overlay networks: containers or virtual machines given their own addressing on top of a physical network
Reaching a machine behind NAT: the tunnel is an outbound connection, which is the technique from the NAT lesson

blocks.title: Watch the routing change
steps: Before connecting, record: ip route     and note your default route
Note your visible address: curl -s https://api.ipify.org ; echo
Connect a VPN, then run ip route again and find the new default and the tunnel interface
Check your visible address again — it should be the gateway's
Run: ip route get 1.1.1.1     and confirm it now goes through the tunnel
Run: ip link show     and compare the tunnel interface's MTU with your physical interface's
Try a large transfer over the tunnel; if it hangs, test with ping -M do at decreasing sizes
Disconnect and confirm the default route and visible address return
blocks.expected: A default route that moves to the tunnel and back, a visible address that changes with it, and a tunnel MTU smaller than the physical one. That last observation connects directly to the layers lesson: the tunnel's own headers are why the usable size shrank, and why VPNs are where MTU problems are most often met.

cheatsheet: A tunnel puts a whole packet inside another packet
The outer header costs space, so a tunnel's usable packet size is smaller
MTU problems show up on VPNs more than anywhere else, for that reason
A VPN moves trust from your local network and provider to the VPN provider
It hides which sites you visit from your provider; it does not make you anonymous to the sites
Full tunnel installs a default route through the tunnel; split tunnel installs specific routes
The full-versus-split difference is entirely the longest-prefix rule at work
Traffic is protected only as far as the gateway — a plain http site stays plain past it
The same mechanism underlies site-to-site links, overlay networks, and reaching machines behind NAT

checkpoint.prompt: Why do large file transfers often hang over a VPN while small requests work?

choices.C: The tunnel's outer header reduces the usable packet size, and the MTU problem from the layers lesson appears
choices.D: Encryption is slower for large data

checkpoint.explanation: Same failure signature as before: small things work, large things hang. The tunnel headers are why the effective size shrank, which is why VPNs are where this is most commonly met.

checkpoint.prompt: You connect to a plain http site through a VPN. Who can read the content?

choices.B: Anyone on the path between the VPN gateway and the site

checkpoint.explanation: The tunnel only protects the first segment. Tunnel encryption and end-to-end encryption protect different segments. Past the gateway the traffic continues exactly as it otherwise would.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the technical difference between a full tunnel and a split tunnel?
checkpoint.explanation: A full tunnel adds a default route through the tunnel, a split tunnel adds only specific ones. It is entirely a routing decision, and you can watch it happen in ip route. The longest-prefix rule then does the rest.

checkpoint.prompt: Which claim about a VPN is accurate?

choices.B: It moves who can observe your traffic from your local network and provider to the VPN provider
choices.C: It encrypts traffic all the way to every site

checkpoint.explanation: That is a genuine and useful improvement on an untrusted network. Sites still identify you by your account, cookies and fingerprinting, and the protection ends at the gateway.
